title: Lateral deformation and defect resistance of compacted silica glass: Quantification of the scratching hardness
text: Silica glass densified under high pressure exhibits markedly different mechanical behavior from its pristine counterpart, yet its resistance to lateral contact damage remains poorly quantified. In this study, we compacted silica glass samples to varying degrees of densification and subjected them to progressive-load micro-scratch tests using a conical indenter. Scratch hardness was derived from residual groove widths, while the onset of lateral cracking and chipping was identified through optical and scanning electron microscopy. Densification increased scratch hardness by up to 45% and substantially delayed the formation of lateral cracks, shifting the dominant deformation mechanism from densification toward shear flow. We propose a simple model linking scratch hardness to the remaining free volume in the glass network. These findings suggest that pre-compaction offers a practical route to improving the surface damage resistance of silica-based components used in optical and display applications.

title: Me or just like me? The role of virtual try-on and physical appearance in apparel M-retailing
text: Virtual try-on (VTO) technology allows mobile shoppers to visualize apparel on a digital representation of themselves, but little is known about whether the realism of that representation matters. Drawing on self-congruity theory, this research examines how the similarity between a VTO avatar and the consumer's own physical appearance shapes product evaluations and purchase intentions in mobile retailing. Across two online experiments, participants used a VTO application featuring either a personalized avatar or a generic model of similar body type. Personalized avatars increased perceived self-congruity and decision confidence, which in turn raised purchase intentions. However, this effect was attenuated among consumers with lower body satisfaction, for whom generic but similar models produced more favorable responses. The findings offer guidance to retailers on when to invest in highly personalized VTO experiences and highlight the role of body image in technology-mediated shopping.

title: Quantitative composition–bioactivity relationships of phosphosilicate glasses: Bearings from the phosphorus content
text: Bioactive phosphosilicate glasses are widely used for bone regeneration, yet the quantitative role of phosphorus content in governing their reactivity is still debated. Here we combine molecular dynamics simulations with in vitro dissolution experiments to examine a series of glasses in which P2O5 content is systematically varied at constant network connectivity. Simulations reveal that phosphorus predominantly forms isolated orthophosphate units that scavenge network-modifying cations, thereby repolymerizing the silicate network. Experimentally, glasses with intermediate phosphorus content exhibited the fastest hydroxyapatite formation in simulated body fluid, whereas higher contents slowed ion release. We establish a composition–bioactivity relationship that accounts for both network connectivity and the cation distribution between silicate and phosphate environments. The resulting framework enables more reliable prediction of bioactivity and supports the rational design of next-generation bioactive glasses.

title: A very brief measure of the Big-Five personality domains
text: Researchers often face severe time constraints that preclude the use of standard multi-item personality inventories. This article reports the development and validation of very brief instruments for assessing the Big-Five personality domains. Using a large undergraduate sample, we compared a five-item and a ten-item measure against established longer inventories. Both brief measures reached adequate levels of convergence with the comprehensive scales, as well as satisfactory test–retest reliability over a six-week interval. Patterns of external correlates and self–observer agreement closely mirrored those obtained with the longer instruments. Although the brief measures are somewhat inferior to standard inventories in terms of internal consistency and discriminant validity, they offer a reasonable alternative when personality is not the primary focus of a study or when assessment time is extremely limited. We discuss the trade-offs involved and provide recommendations for appropriate use.

title: Inter-subject transfer learning for EEG-based mental fatigue recognition
text: Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a promising, non-invasive signal for detecting mental fatigue, but large inter-subject variability severely limits the generalization of models trained on one group of individuals. In this paper, we propose an inter-subject transfer learning framework that aligns the feature distributions of source and target subjects before classification. EEG recordings were collected from participants performing a prolonged cognitive task, and spectral and connectivity features were extracted from multiple frequency bands. We apply domain adaptation techniques, including covariance alignment and adversarial feature learning, to reduce the distribution shift between subjects. Experiments under a leave-one-subject-out protocol show that the proposed approach improves fatigue recognition accuracy by more than 10 percentage points over models without adaptation, while requiring only a small amount of unlabeled target data. These results highlight the potential of transfer learning for building practical, calibration-light fatigue monitoring systems.

title: Effectiveness of product return-prevention instruments: Empirical evidence
text: Product returns impose substantial costs on online retailers, yet evidence on the effectiveness of instruments designed to prevent them remains scarce. Using transaction-level data from a large European fashion retailer, this study evaluates a set of return-prevention instruments, including detailed size advice, product reviews, and enhanced product imagery. We exploit staggered introductions of these instruments across product categories to estimate their causal effects on return rates and net sales. Results indicate that size advice and customer reviews significantly reduce return rates without lowering purchase rates, whereas additional product images have no measurable effect. The impact of the instruments is strongest for first-time customers and for products with high size uncertainty. These findings help managers allocate resources toward return-prevention measures that improve profitability and offer insights into the informational drivers of returns.

title: Testing measurement invariance of composites using partial least squares
text: Comparing structural relationships across groups requires that the constructs be measured equivalently in each group, yet procedures for assessing measurement invariance in composite models estimated with partial least squares (PLS) have been lacking. This paper introduces a three-step procedure for testing the measurement invariance of composites in PLS path modeling. The procedure assesses configural invariance, compositional invariance, and the equality of composite means and variances, using permutation-based tests that do not rely on distributional assumptions. We demonstrate the approach with an empirical example from customer satisfaction research and evaluate its performance through a simulation study. Results show that the procedure reliably detects violations of invariance while maintaining appropriate error rates. Researchers using PLS multigroup analysis should establish measurement invariance prior to comparing path coefficients to ensure that observed differences reflect genuine structural effects rather than measurement artifacts.

title: Try online before you buy: How does shopping with augmented reality affect brand responses and personal data disclosure
text: Augmented reality (AR) applications allow consumers to virtually try products before purchasing, but their consequences for brand perceptions and privacy behavior are not well understood. This study investigates how shopping with an AR try-on application, compared with a conventional website, influences consumer responses toward the brand and willingness to disclose personal information. In a between-subjects experiment, participants shopped for eyewear using either an AR mirror or a standard product page. AR shopping increased perceived enjoyment and spatial presence, which enhanced brand attitudes and purchase intentions. Notably, participants in the AR condition were also more willing to share personal data with the retailer, an effect mediated by heightened enjoyment rather than increased trust. These findings point to the persuasive power of immersive retail technologies and raise important questions about informed consent in AR-based commerce.

title: The role of data privacy in marketing
text: As firms collect increasingly detailed information about consumers, data privacy has become a central concern for marketing practice and research. This article reviews the conceptual foundations of privacy and synthesizes research on how consumers, firms, and regulators navigate the trade-offs inherent in data-driven marketing. We discuss the privacy paradox, the effects of perceived control and transparency on consumer responses, and the competitive implications of data access. Drawing on theories from economics, psychology, and ethics, we propose a framework that links data collection practices to consumer vulnerability and firm performance. We argue that privacy failures can damage trust and long-term customer relationships, whereas responsible data stewardship can serve as a source of competitive advantage. The article concludes with an agenda for future research on privacy regulation, emerging technologies, and the ethical boundaries of personalization.

title: I wear, therefore I am: investigating sneakerhead culture, social identity, and brand preference among men
text: Sneaker collecting has evolved from a niche hobby into a global consumer subculture, yet the identity processes that sustain it remain underexplored. This study examines how membership in the sneakerhead community shapes male consumers' social identity and brand preferences. Drawing on social identity theory, we conducted in-depth interviews with committed collectors and surveyed a broader sample of male sneaker consumers. Findings reveal that sneakers function as markers of authenticity, cultural knowledge, and status within the community, and that brand preference is driven less by product performance than by brand heritage, scarcity, and alignment with subcultural values. Identification with the community strengthened loyalty toward brands perceived as authentic participants in sneaker culture. The study contributes to research on consumption subcultures and offers implications for brands seeking to engage passionate, identity-driven consumer communities.

title: A molecular dynamics study of the effect of water diffusion into bio-active phosphate-based glass surfaces on their dissolution behaviour
text: Phosphate-based glasses are attractive biomaterials because their dissolution rate can be tailored for controlled ion release, but the atomistic mechanisms that initiate dissolution remain unclear. In this work, we use classical molecular dynamics simulations to investigate water diffusion into the surfaces of phosphate-based glasses with varying calcium and sodium content. Simulations reveal that water molecules readily penetrate the near-surface region, where they preferentially coordinate with sodium ions and disrupt phosphate chain connectivity. Glasses with higher sodium content exhibited faster water ingress and greater surface hydration, consistent with their higher experimental dissolution rates, whereas calcium-rich compositions formed more stable surface layers. These results provide molecular-level insight into the early stages of glass degradation and support compositional strategies for tuning the dissolution behaviour of phosphate-based glasses in biomedical applications.

title: Is augmented reality technology an effective tool for e-commerce? An interactivity and vividness perspective
text: Augmented reality (AR) is increasingly adopted by online retailers, but evidence of its effectiveness as an e-commerce tool remains limited. Building on the concepts of interactivity and vividness, this study examines how AR product presentations influence consumers' attitudes and purchase intentions compared with traditional web-based presentations. An online experiment was conducted in which participants evaluated products presented through either an AR interface or a standard product page. Results show that AR enhances perceived interactivity and vividness, which in turn increase perceived informativeness and enjoyment, ultimately improving attitudes toward the product and purchase intention. The effect of vividness was particularly strong for products whose evaluation depends on visual and spatial attributes. The findings contribute to the understanding of how AR creates value in online shopping and offer practical guidance for retailers considering AR investments.

title: Uniting the tribes: Using text for marketing insight
text: Words are part of almost every marketplace interaction, from online reviews and social media posts to customer service exchanges and firm communications. Text analysis offers marketing researchers a powerful way to extract insight from this growing body of language data, yet its use remains fragmented across disciplines. This article provides an overview of automated text analysis and its applications in marketing. We describe how text can be used to understand consumers, firms, and markets, review common methods ranging from dictionary-based approaches to topic modeling and machine learning, and discuss key issues in measurement, validity, and inference. We highlight opportunities for collaboration across research traditions that study language from different perspectives. The article aims to unite these tribes by offering a common framework and practical guidance for researchers seeking to use text to generate novel marketing insights.

title: An integrative review of sensory marketing: Engaging the senses to affect perception, judgment and behavior
text: Sensory marketing refers to marketing that engages consumers' senses and affects their perception, judgment, and behavior. This article provides an integrative review of research on sensory marketing, covering the five senses of touch, smell, sound, taste, and vision. We discuss how sensory cues influence consumers through both conscious and nonconscious processes, and how sensory perceptions can shape attitudes, memory, and choice. Drawing on research in psychology and consumer behavior, we highlight the role of grounded cognition in explaining sensory effects and identify the conditions under which sensory cues are most influential. We also examine the interactions among different senses and the implications of multisensory experiences for product and retail design. The review concludes by outlining open questions and directions for future research on how marketers can leverage sensory experiences to create value for consumers.

title: Estimation and inference of heterogeneous treatment effects using random forests
text: Many scientific and policy questions require estimating how the effect of a treatment varies across individuals with different characteristics. This paper develops a nonparametric causal forest for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects that extends the random forest algorithm of Breiman. We show that, under suitable conditions, causal forest predictions are pointwise consistent for the true treatment effect and have an asymptotically Gaussian distribution, which enables valid confidence intervals. The key ingredient is the use of honest trees, in which separate subsamples are used to construct the splits and to estimate effects within leaves. Simulation experiments indicate that causal forests outperform classical nearest-neighbor matching methods, particularly in settings with many covariates. The method is broadly applicable to observational studies and randomized experiments in which researchers seek to understand treatment effect heterogeneity.

title: Augmenting the eye of the beholder: exploring the strategic potential of augmented reality to enhance online service experiences
text: Augmented reality (AR) is emerging as a technology capable of transforming how customers experience services online, yet its strategic potential for service providers has not been systematically examined. This article explores how AR can enhance online service experiences by augmenting customers' perception of physical reality with virtual elements. Drawing on the concept of situated cognition, we develop a framework describing how AR applications differ in the degree to which they embed virtual content in the customer's physical environment. Through a series of studies, we show that AR can increase perceived value of the service experience and influence decision comfort and behavioral intentions. We discuss strategic implications for service firms considering AR deployment and outline directions for future research on immersive service technologies.

title: False-positive psychology: Undisclosed flexibility in data collection and analysis allows presenting anything as significant
text: Despite widely accepted standards for statistical significance, researchers routinely make many decisions during data collection and analysis that can inflate the rate of false-positive findings. In this article, we show that undisclosed flexibility in choices such as when to stop collecting data, which measures to report, which conditions to compare, and which covariates to include makes it surprisingly easy to obtain statistically significant evidence for a false hypothesis. Using computer simulations and two experiments, we demonstrate how combining these common practices can raise the actual false-positive rate far above the nominal five percent level. We then propose a simple, low-cost set of disclosure requirements for authors and guidelines for reviewers. These recommendations would make research practices more transparent and substantially reduce the publication of false-positive results without imposing a significant burden on researchers.
